subject: Medicine
summary: Septic arthritis is an infection of a joint space that can rapidly destroy cartilage and bone. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent permanent disability and death.

sections.p: Septic arthritis is the invasion of a synovial joint by pathogenic microorganisms, most often bacteria, leading to inflammation and joint damage.
b: Diagnosis requires synovial fluid analysis showing high white cells (>50,000/µL), positive Gram stain or culture, and clinical signs of acute joint inflammation.

t.b: Does the joint contain infection? High leukocyte count, neutrophil predominance, low glucose, high protein, and positive Gram stain/culture confirm infection.
Is there an effusion to sample? Aspiration provides fluid for analysis; if unavailable, proceed with imaging and empiric therapy based on clinical suspicion.

sections.p: Severity is staged by the extent of joint destruction and systemic involvement, using the Kocher criteria and imaging findings.
b: Mild: limited effusion, normal imaging.
Moderate: effusion with early cartilage loss on ultrasound/MRI.
Severe: bone erosion, osteomyelitis, or septic shock.

sections.p: Bacterial pathogens dominate, with patient‑specific risk factors influencing the likely organism.
b: Staphylococcus aureus – most common overall.
Streptococcus species – especially in children and post‑viral patients.
Salmonella – in sickle‑cell disease.
Gram‑negative bacilli – in immunocompromised or urinary tract infection sources.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis – in endemic regions or HIV.
Fungal organisms – in severe immunosuppression.

sections.p: Patients develop an acutely painful, swollen, warm joint that is often unable to bear weight.
b: Rapid onset (hours‑days) of severe joint pain.
Visible swelling, erythema, and warmth.
Fever or systemic signs in most adults; may be absent in immunocompromised.

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm infection, identify the pathogen, and assess joint damage.
b: Blood cultures detect bacteremia in 30‑50% of cases.
Plain radiographs show late bone changes; early imaging is usually normal.

t.b: Is there systemic bacteremia? Positive cultures guide antimicrobial choice; negative cultures do not exclude joint infection.
Is there an effusion? Detects fluid for aspiration; may show synovial thickening.
Is there adjacent osteomyelitis or soft‑tissue spread? Shows early bone marrow edema and helps surgical planning.

sections.p: Unchecked infection can lead to irreversible joint damage and life‑threatening sepsis.
b: Rapid joint destruction → loss of function.
Septic shock, multi‑organ failure.
Adjacent osteomyelitis or abscess formation.
Chronic disability, especially in weight‑bearing joints.

sections.p: Early joint drainage and appropriate antibiotics are the cornerstones of care.
b: Urgent arthrocentesis or surgical washout to remove purulent material.
Empiric IV antibiotics covering Staph aureus, Streptococci, and Gram‑negatives (e.g., a first‑generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin in MRSA‑prevalent areas).
Tailor antibiotics once culture results are available; avoid agents with poor bone penetration or high nephrotoxicity in renal impairment.
Supportive care: analgesia, fluid resuscitation, and monitoring for sepsis.

sections.p: Patients need monitoring for treatment response and strategies to reduce recurrence.
b: Repeat joint aspiration if clinical improvement is not evident within 48‑72 h.
Physical therapy after infection control to restore range of motion.
Vaccination (e.g., pneumococcal, influenza) and management of underlying conditions (e.g., sickle‑cell disease, HIV) to lower future risk.

sections.p: Several non‑infectious joint conditions mimic septic arthritis.
b: Crystal arthropathies (gout, pseudogout) – crystals on microscopy, usually lower leukocyte count.
Reactive arthritis – sterile joint after infection elsewhere, negative cultures.
Rheumatoid arthritis flare – symmetric polyarthritis, serology positive, no purulent fluid.

sections.p: Certain findings may give a false sense of security.
b: Normal white‑cell count in synovial fluid early in infection.
Negative Gram stain despite positive culture – low bacterial load.
Low‑grade fever in immunocompromised patients may mask severe infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening joint pain and swelling
Inability to bear weight on the affected limb
Signs of systemic sepsis (hypotension, tachycardia, confusion)

faq.a: It provides fluid for definitive diagnosis and relieves pressure, improving pain and preventing cartilage loss.

faq.q: Can septic arthritis be treated without surgery?
faq.a: Small joints may respond to needle aspiration alone, but large joints usually need surgical washout for adequate drainage.

faq.q: What is the role of antibiotics after drainage?
faq.a: Antibiotics eradicate residual bacteria, prevent spread, and reduce the risk of chronic infection.

exam: List the three most common bacterial causes of septic arthritis and a key risk factor for each.
Describe the synovial fluid findings that differentiate septic arthritis from crystal arthropathy.
Outline the initial management steps for a patient with suspected septic arthritis of the knee.
